name: dotslash
why: Turns executables into small manifest files that fetch binaries on demand, a curious idea about what a runnable file can be.

brief.what_it_is: DotSlash is a command-line tool, invoked as `dotslash`, that replaces a set of platform-specific, heavyweight executables with one small, readable text file. You make the file executable and give it a `#!/usr/bin/env dotslash` shebang. The file is a JSON-like manifest (the README example uses `//` comments) that lists, per platform, the download URL, size, hash digest, archive format and the path inside the archive. When you run the file, DotSlash fetches, decompresses and verifies the right binary for your platform. The homepage also says it provides tools for generating DotSlash files from GitHub releases.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to keep executables in source control without bloating the repository, so build toolchains and other tools can be checked into the repo. That reduces dependence on the host environment and helps with reproducible builds.
brief.how_it_works: The manifest names a platform-keyed set of entries, each with a provider URL, a blake3 digest and size, and the archive path of the binary. On first run DotSlash downloads, decompresses and verifies the matching archive, which is the small delay the README mentions, and later runs are near-instant. The README points to a docs page on execution for the details, which I did not fetch.

commands_seen.context: Shebang line that goes at the top of the manifest file so the OS hands the file to dotslash.
Marks the manifest file as executable so it can be run directly, per the README's instructions.
Example of running the manifest-wrapped Node.js exactly as before; the README shows output v18.16.0.

brief.install_notes: The README gives no install steps beyond a link to the installation page on dotslash-cli.com/docs/installation/, which I did not fetch. It assumes `dotslash` is on your $PATH. Each user must chmod +x the manifest file. No accounts or runtimes are mentioned.
brief.standout: Instead of a shell wrapper plus several binaries, a single text file is the executable, and it fetches the correct binary per platform on demand. Storing the manifest in git keeps the repo small while still vendoring tools like Node.js.
brief.status: unknown. The GitHub page shows an MIT OR Apache-2.0 license badge and a build workflow badge pointing at main, but I saw no release date, last commit date or maintenance note in the text I could read.
brief.caveats: The README example pins Node.js v18.19.0 in the manifest but its sample output reads v18.16.0, which looks like a typo or a stale example. The first run has a download and verify delay. The Rust performance claim appears only on the homepage, not in the README. I did not read the installation or execution docs, so platform support and setup details are unverified.
quotes: DotSlash (`dotslash`) is a command-line tool that lets you represent a set of platform-specific, heavyweight executables with an equivalent small, easy-to-read text file.
This paves the way for checking build toolchains and other tools directly into the repo, reducing dependencies on the host environment and thereby facilitating reproducible builds.
DotSlash is written in Rust so it can run your executables quickly and transparently.
